races.title: State House, District 37
races.note: The top two finishers from the Nov 3, 2026 count. Everyone else in this race is coming.

cands.name: Erin Pare
cands.bio: Republican state representative for North Carolina House District 37 (southern Wake County) since January 2021. Owns a Play-It-Again-Sports store in Holly Springs and founded the Holly Strings Youth Orchestra. Earlier spent seven years in Washington, D.C. government affairs, including as director of the Regulatory Improvement Council.

endorsements.text: Her campaign site says she is endorsed by the Police Benevolent Association and by the retired police chiefs of Fuquay-Varina and Holly Springs, and that she was named "Defender of Public Safety" by the NC Sheriff's Association.

cands.gaps: The sources give no year for her move to North Carolina, so her ties to the state could not be scored. Her campaign site's descriptions of bills she passed or sponsored were not checked against legislative records, so they appear only as her own statements. Her site says she passed a bill requiring data centers to supply their own power, but it does not describe a ban, moratorium or preemption, so it is not counted for or against any position on data centers. Nothing was found on her positions on H-1B visas, institutional or foreign land buyers, or red-flag laws. Ballotpedia lists no endorsements for her in 2024 or 2026, and she did not complete Ballotpedia's 2022, 2024 or 2026 candidate surveys. No controversies were found in the pages reviewed.

score.why: Raised $0, under $5,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Has served in the NC House since 2021 and chairs the House Appropriations Committee. Earlier she spent seven years in Washington, D.C. government affairs and regulatory policy, owns a small business, and was vice-chair of the Holly Springs Board of Adjustment.
qual.why: Five years of legislative service, a policy and regulatory career, and business ownership fit the work of writing law and the state budget. The committee chair role was not counted.
qual.label: Five years of legislative service, a policy and regulatory career, and business ownership fit the work of writing law and the state budget. The committee chair role was not counted.

end-homestead-tax.evidence: Her campaign site says she leads the House push for property tax reduction and reform, filed legislation to expand the homestead exemption for seniors, and sponsored a bill to limit property tax increases. These are her own claims, not checked against bill records.

slow-growth-protect-land.evidence: Her campaign site says she passed legislation halting ETJ expansion in Wake County, included farmland preservation funding in the 2026 budget, and supports growth only when school and infrastructure capacity come first. These are her own claims, not checked against bill records.

workers-first.evidence: In her 2020 Ballotpedia survey she listed fighting sanctuary sheriffs and opposing illegal immigration as priorities.

back-police-order.evidence: Her campaign site says she passed HB 307 (Iryna's Law) tightening pretrial release for people accused of violent offenses, and as budget chair secured the highest law enforcement pay raises in state history.

second-amendment.evidence: In her 2020 Ballotpedia survey she listed defending Second Amendment rights as a key campaign message.

pro-life.evidence: In her 2020 Ballotpedia survey she described herself as pro-life and listed it as a key campaign message.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: In her 2020 Ballotpedia survey she said she is pro-school choice.

prio.label: Matches 7 of 7 priorities; 0 backed by their record, 7 only promised

land_positions.quote_or_summary: Her campaign site says she supports a responsible approach to growth, making sure school capacity and critical infrastructure are in place ahead of growth approved by local governments, and that she passed legislation halting ETJ expansion in Wake County.

cands.name: Winn Decker
cands.bio: Democrat from Fuquay-Varina with a Ph.D. in public administration from NC State. He works in education and workforce policy, including time at the Hunt Institute, and is reported to work for Common App. He won North Carolina House District 37 in 2026, defeating incumbent Erin Paré. First elected office.

endorsements.text: Listed endorsements include Run for Something and NC Public School Champions (a Sway voting group), along with several other voter-guide groups.

cands.gaps: His birthplace and exact year of arrival in North Carolina are not given in the sources. We found no stated position on data centers, foreign or institutional land buying, immigration or H-1B visas, guns, or abortion. He has held no prior public office, so there is no record of legislative actions. His current employer is described differently across sources, and his job titles and dates are not detailed.

local.label: Roots 40: He was raised in rural northwest Tennessee and says he made Wake County home over a decade ago while earning his Ph.D. at NC State, so he arrived as an adult 10-25 years ago.

score.why: Raised $0, under $5,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Policy career in education and workforce policy, including the Hunt Institute, where he worked with governors, legislators and state leaders; a Ph.D. in public administration focused on education policy and public budgeting; reportedly now at Common App. He has held no elected office.
qual.why: Policy and budget-focused work and training fit the middle band for policy staff. There is no prior legislative service or local elected office to move him higher.
qual.label: Policy and budget-focused work and training fit the middle band for policy staff. There is no prior legislative service or local elected office to move him higher.

end-homestead-tax.evidence: His campaign site lists "Reduce property taxes and make housing more affordable" among the things he will work for. It does not specify homestead elimination.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: His campaign site pledges to support public schools and raise teacher pay. He did not state a position on vouchers or charters in the pages reviewed.

back-police-order.evidence: His campaign site pledges to adequately fund law enforcement and first responders.

slow-growth-protect-land.evidence: His campaign site says he will advocate for smarter development and infrastructure that keeps up with growth. His Ballotpedia survey says growth should strengthen communities, not overwhelm them. Neither mentions land conservation or limits on rezoning.

prio.label: Matches 4 of 4 priorities; 0 backed by their record, 4 only promised

roots.summary: He was raised in rural northwest Tennessee and says he made Wake County home over a decade ago while earning his Ph.D. at NC State, so he arrived as an adult 10-25 years ago.
